name: Guianese Creole French
confidence_why: One first-hand description, checked against the source; 4 other works consulted do not discuss stress.

tone_statements.citation: Lewis, André Alexus. 2024. Linguistic Features of French Guiana Creole: Analyzing Phonology, Morphology, and Syntax Compared to Standard French and Other Creoles. International Journal of Research and Innovation in Social Science (IJRISS) 8(7): 3379-3393. RSIS International.
tone_statements.quote: Table 1: Phonological Features of French Guiana Creole vs. Standard French ... Tone | Present | Absent | ba [bá] | Stress Patterns | Variable | Fixed | cadeau [ka'do] ... Although Standard French is not tonal, Creole may differ significantly in comparisons of pitch. ... Tonal characteristics that are drawn from African and indigenous languages give FGC's phonological system an additional level of complexity, enhancing both its expressive and aesthetic qualities. In FGC, tonal patterns serve as markers of grammatical categories, discourse functions, and lexical distinctions.
tone_statements.locator: HTML full text: Table 1 'Phonological Features of French Guiana Creole vs. Standard French' and the paragraph after it; last paragraph of the discussion before 'Conclusions' (print pp. 3379-3393, exact page not determinable from HTML)
tone_statements.check: quotation verified in source (minor differences in wording)
tone_statements.summary: Asserts 'tone present' with lexical and grammatical functions but names no tones, no contrasts and no tone-bearing unit; simultaneously calls stress 'variable'; unusable as a description.

audit.reasoning: (1) Quote: verbatim confirmed in the APiCS survey chapter 52, §3 Phonology (file downloaded now; nothing was held before). (2) Deciding source: a 2013 atlas survey sketch by a language specialist (Pfänder), one unargued sentence; first-hand but not a phonology study. (3) Better descriptions exist and are not yet obtained: Saint-Jacques-Fauquenoy 1972 (structural description incl. phonology), Fauquenoy 1967 (ORSTOM phonology), Jennings & Pfänder 2018 ch. 3, Patzelt 2025 handbook chapter; all print-only or paywalled. Open items downloaded now (Wiesinger 2026 LGMEF fiche; Saint-Quentin 1872) are silent on word stress. (4) Final stress is the expected pattern for a French-lexifier creole and nothing seen contradicts the 'fixed-dominant final' coding; the realistic risk from a fuller source is a refinement (accent described as group/phrase-final rather than lexical), not a different syllable. Hence status
audit.second_reader_evidence: The quotation was checked again: independent. (APiCS Online survey ch. 52 'Guyanais', S. Pfaender; print = Michaelis et al. eds. 2013, Survey vol. 2, 220-228). Stripped text, section '3. Phonology': '.. lateral approximant l j <y> w Word stress is always on the last syllable. An orthography has been proposed and promoted by a group of creolists called GEREC-F..' -> the record's sources[0].text is verbatim, locator = §3 Phonology, sentence directly after Table 3 (Consonants). the compilers locator is correct.
